title: Pompeii Wardrobe Opens After Almost 2,000 Years
paragraphs: For almost two millennia, a wooden cupboard in the ancient Roman city of Pompeii stayed shut. Now the Archaeological Park of Pompeii has announced that archaeologists have opened it, offering a rare glimpse of ordinary life shortly before Mount Vesuvius buried the city in the year 79. The house stands on the Via dell'Abbondanza and is tentatively linked to a man called Cornelius Maximus; its facade was excavated in 1912, but the rooms behind it have only recently been studied.

The cupboard held a necklace of at least 24 small amulets made of bone, glass paste, faience and rock crystal, including images of the gods Mercury and Bes. This type of necklace was given to Roman children, so it may have belonged to a child, or to an adult who kept it from childhood. Alongside it were 38 bronze coins, tweezers, a perfume bottle, an incense burner and a wooden box with lead weights, which hints at a trader in the household.

Researchers suspect the occupants left in a hurry and never returned, but the evidence is circumstantial. “Pompeii is not just a place of great works of art,” director Gabriel Zuchtriegel said, adding that everyday objects restore the human dimension of the past. He also cautioned that the identity of the residents cannot be reconstructed with certainty, and it remains unclear whether the family died in the eruption or fled and could not return.

questions.q: Why is the necklace especially interesting?
questions.a: It is a type given to Roman children, so it may link to a child or to someone's childhood.

questions.q: What do the lead weights suggest?
questions.a: That someone in the household was involved in trade.

questions.q: Why is the idea of a hurried escape only a suspicion?
questions.a: Because the evidence is circumstantial and the residents' fate is unknown.
